pointers.sentence: `USE_TZ` has been true by default since 5.0, so a project that never set it now works with aware datetimes; `DEFAULT_AUTO_FIELD` has named `BigAutoField` since 6.0, so a model with no primary key of its own, in an application that names no other, gets a 64-bit one (`django/conf/global_settings.py`); and since 6.2 `JsonResponse` serialises a list without being told that it is safe (`django/http/response.py:JsonResponse.__init__`).

Django makes a feature release about every eight months, and the third of each series is a long-term support release, which receives security fixes for a guaranteed period, typically three years (`docs/internals/release-process.txt`).
5.0 came on 4 December 2023, 5.1 on 7 August 2024, 5.2 on 2 April 2025, 6.0 on 3 December 2025 and 6.1 on 5 August 2026 (`docs/releases/`).

Following DEP 20, the releases after it, once planned as 7.0 and 7.1, are Django 2028 and Django 2029, calendar versions with no minor number (`docs/releases/6.2.txt`; [Django's version: `VersionTuple` and `get_version`](utils/version.md)).

A fix for a critical bug in the newest feature release, a crash, a regression, a major fault in a new feature, goes to that release's branch as well as to main; a fix for a security issue or for the loss of data goes to main, to the last two feature releases and to any long-term release still supported (`docs/internals/release-process.txt`).

A feature release may change behaviour outright, and its notes list each such change as backwards incompatible; the release process allows these where a path through deprecation is not possible or not worth its cost (`docs/internals/release-process.txt`).
A name that moved is answered by a module's `__getattr__`, as `MiddlewareMixin` is in its old module (`django/utils/deprecation.py:__getattr__`).
A parameter made keyword-only takes its old position for the period through `deprecate_posargs` (`django/utils/deprecation.py:deprecate_posargs`).

An override written for the old signature is found by inspecting it: a model's own `from_db` that accepts neither `fetch_mode` nor arbitrary keywords is called without the mode, with a warning (`django/db/models/query.py:_get_from_db`).

A class that defines an old hook is caught as it is made, in `__init_subclass__`, as a field class that defines the old placeholder method is (`django/db/models/fields/__init__.py:Field.__init_subclass__`).
These are the ones at this commit (`django/conf/global_settings.py`).

`URLIZE_ASSUME_HTTPS`, from 6.0, makes `urlize` assume `"https"` for the bare domains it links, a name beginning with www. or ending in .com, .org or one of five others, before Django 2028 makes that the default (`django/utils/html.py:Urlizer.handle_word`).

`USE_BLANK_CHOICE_DASH`, from 6.1, brings back the dashes that the blank choice of a model field's choices and of a `ModelChoiceField` used to show (`django/db/models/utils.py:get_blank_choice_label`).

`SIGNED_COOKIE_LEGACY_SALT_FALLBACK` came with a fix to the salts of signed cookies in 5.2.15 and 6.0.6, and when true lets a signed cookie made under the old salt be read; its default became false in 6.1 (`django/core/signing.py:_unsign_cookie`).

Setting either of the last two warns: in a settings module always, and through `configure` or an override when the code that sets it is outside Django (`django/conf/__init__.py:Settings.__init__`, `django/conf/__init__.py:_show_settings_deprecation_warning`; [What changed in settings, startup and the commands](changes/startup-and-commands.md)).

A field may have a default that the database supplies, `Field.db_default` (5.0), or be a column the database generates, `GeneratedField` (5.0), which since 6.0 a save reads back with the statement's `"RETURNING"` clause where the backend has one (`django/db/models/fields/generated.py:GeneratedField`, `django/db/models/base.py:Model._save_table`).

A field may have a default that the database supplies, `Field.db_default` (5.0), or be a column the database generates, `GeneratedField` (5.0), which since 6.0 a save reads back with the statement's `"RETURNING"` clause where the backend has one (`django/db/models/fields/generated.py:GeneratedField`, `django/db/models/base.py:Model._save_table`).

An `on_delete` may leave the work to the database's own `ON DELETE` clause, with `DB_CASCADE`, `DB_SET_NULL` or `DB_SET_DEFAULT` (6.1), and the collector of a delete then passes over the relation (`django/db/models/deletion.py:DatabaseOnDelete`).

Since 6.1 that is one of three **fetch modes**, `FETCH_ONE`, beside `FETCH_PEERS`, which fetches it at once for the other instances that the same run of the queryset made, and `FETCH_RAISE`, which refuses (`django/db/models/fetch_modes.py`; [Deferred fields and fetch modes in a queryset](querysets/deferred.md)).
Until then `mailers["default"]` is built from `EMAIL_BACKEND` when a project does not define `MAILERS` (`django/core/mail/handler.py:MailersHandler.create_connection`).

Aware datetimes (5.0), 64-bit automatic keys (6.0), `"https"` as the scheme a form's URL field assumes (6.0; `django/forms/fields.py:URLField`) and the urlize filter will assume (Django 2028), SHA-256 as `salted_hmac`'s default algorithm (Django 2028), and an iteration count for the PBKDF2 password hasher raised in every feature release, from 720,000 in 5.0 to 1,800,000 at this commit (`django/contrib/auth/hashers.py:PBKDF2PasswordHasher`).
